---
title: Should we move the office?
---
- Should we move the office?
  - Stay where we are
    - For: the lease is cheap and everyone knows the way
    - Against: no room for the two people we are hiring in January
  - Take the floor above
    - For: twice the room, the same address
    - Against: the rent goes up by a third^[From £2,400 a month to £3,200, on a five-year lease from 1 January 2027.]
  - Go remote
    - For: no rent at all; hire anywhere
    - Against: the workshop needs a room with a bench in it
  - Decide by Friday 30 October {.to label=then}

docs.text:
---
title: The link is the document
---
- The link is the document
  - The problem {label="5 min"}
    - A file needs a place to live, an account to reach it, a server to keep it
    - Sharing a file is sharing a place
  - The idea {label="10 min"}
    - Put the whole document after the # in the address
    - Nothing is sent anywhere; the browser never shares the part after the #^[Browsers keep the fragment to themselves: it is not in the request a server receives.]
    - Copy the link and you have copied the file
  - What it means {label="5 min"}
    - No sign-up, no saving, no servers to trust
    - A document is as private as the link
    - Try it: tinylittleoffice.com

docs.name: outline/essay
docs.text:
---
title: Is a four-day week good for a small business?
---
- Is a four-day week good for a small business?
  - The thesis
    - Yes, for a business that sells its work and not its hours behind a counter
  - The same work in less time
    - Of the 61 companies in the British trial of 2022, 56 kept the shorter week^[Autonomy, *The results are in: the UK’s four-day week pilot*, February 2023.]
    - Fewer meetings, and shorter ones, are most of the time saved
  - People stay
    - At our studio two of seven left in 2025; none has in 2026
    - Hiring and training a designer costs us about three months of their pay
  - The objection
    - A shop has to open five or six days, whoever is tired
  - The answer
    - Stagger the days off: the doors open six days, each person works four
  - Conclusion
    - Try it for one quarter, measure the work done, and decide on the numbers

~ The objection -> The thesis: tests
~ The answer -> The objection: meets

---
title: Shade at bus stops: a research plan
---
- Do street trees cool a bus stop?
  - The question
    - How much cooler, on a July afternoon, is a stop under a tree than one in full sun?
    - Why it matters: the council plants about 400 street trees a year and has to choose where
  - Method
    1. Choose 20 pairs of stops on the same roads, one shaded and one not
    2. Log the air and the bench temperature every ten minutes from a sensor on each shelter
    3. Count who is waiting at 8 am, 1 pm and 5 pm on four weekdays
  - Budget

```sheet {depth=2}
---
title: Budget
---
Item | Count:number | Each:money | Cost:money
--- | --- | --- | ---
Temperature loggers, four of them spares | 44 | 38 | =B1*C1
Shelter mounts and ties | 44 | 4.50 | =B2*C2
Bus fares for the counts | 160 | 2 | =B3*C3
Storing the data for a year | 1 | 60 | =B4*C4
Total |  |  | =SUM(D1:D4)

```

  - Timeline
    - October to December 2026: choose the stops; ask the council’s leave
    - January to May 2027: buy the loggers and test them on two stops
    - June to August 2027: measure
    - September 2027: write it up for the council and the journal
  - Risks
    - A logger is taken or broken: four spares are in the budget
    - A cool summer: run it again in 2028
  - Reading
    - Why a city is warmer than its fields^[T. R. Oke, *Boundary Layer Climates*, second edition, Routledge, 1987, chapter 8.]

---
title: Urban Ecology, autumn 2026
---
- Urban Ecology (ENV 214), autumn term 2026
  - The course
    - Thursdays 14:00 to 16:00, Room B12, from 1 October to 3 December
    - Dr Amara Okafor; office hours Tuesdays 11:00 to 12:00, Room C4
  - Week by week
    1. The city as a habitat
    2. Soil under the pavement
    3. Street trees and who plants them
    4. Pigeons, foxes and other neighbours
    5. Water: drains, rivers in pipes, rain gardens
    6. Field week: a survey of one block, in pairs
    7. Heat islands
    8. Weeds, walls and wastelands
    9. Light at night
    10. Designing for wildlife; what the survey found
  - How it is marked
    - A field journal, one entry a week, due 10 December: **40%**
    - The block survey, written up in pairs: **30%**
    - An exam on 14 January 2027: **30%**^[Work handed in late loses 5% a day for five days, unless agreed with Dr Okafor before the deadline.]
  - Reading
    - O. L. Gilbert, *The Ecology of Urban Habitats*, chapters 1 to 4 by week 3

---
title: The Lighthouse Keeper
---
- The Lighthouse Keeper
  - The people
    - Mara Quinn
      - Thirty-four, a sound engineer from Dublin who has stopped sleeping
    - Finn Gallagher
      - Seventy-one, keeper of the light for forty years, leaving when the winter ends
    - Nell Hanrahan
      - Captain of the ferry; knew Finn’s wife, Orla, before anyone did
  - Act one: Arrival
    - The ferry
      - Mara takes the last boat of the season out to the island^[Set in the winter of 1987, the year before the light was automated.]
    - The keeper
      - Finn shows her the lamp and will not say why he is leaving
  - Act two: Winter
    - The storm
      - The light fails on the worst night of the year, and Mara climbs to it alone
    - The letters
      - A box under the stairs: forty years of letters Finn wrote to Orla and never sent
  - Act three: Spring
    - The first ferry
      - Nell brings the new keeper, and Mara decides whether to be on the boat back

~ Mara Quinn -> The letters: finds
~ Finn Gallagher -- The storm: his last
~ Nell Hanrahan -> The first ferry: brings the new keeper

---
title: Small Rooms
---
- Small Rooms: living well in less space
  - Part one: Less
    - One in, one out
      - A full shelf is a shelf that works; the rule that keeps it full and no fuller
    - Furniture that folds
      - A table for two that seats eight, and the joiner in Leith who makes them
  - Part two: Light
    - Mirrors, and where not to hang them
      - Opposite a window doubles the light; opposite the bed doubles the mess
    - The colour of a north-facing room
      - Warm whites, and why the brightest white looks grey there
  - Part three: Living
    - Guests
      - A sofa bed, a rule about towels, and three nights at most
    - When it is time to move
      - The signs a small room has stopped being enough, and what to look for next
